stories.headline: Govt Teachers Can Be Deployed As BLOs For Election-Related Duties, Including SIR Work: Allahabad High Court
stories.title: Govt Teachers Can Be Deployed As BLOs For Election-Related Duties, Including SIR Work: Allahabad High Court
stories.summary: HC says BLO duties fall within the RTE Act's exception permitting teachers to be deployed for election-related work.
reasons: corroboration: single independent source -> medium confidence
article_sentences: HC says BLO duties fall within the RTE Act's exception permitting teachers to be deployed for election-related work.
The Allahabad High Court has observed that government teachers can be assigned election-related duties as Booth Level.
Officers (BLOs), including work pertaining to preparation, revision and correction of electoral rolls.

A bench of Justice Vinod Diwakar referred to Section 27 of the Right of Children to Free and Compulsory Education Act, 2009 (RTE Act), which expressly permits the deployment of teachers for election-related duties and that BLO duties fall within this exception.

Rejecting the petitioners' contention that their deployment violated Article 21-A of the Constitution, the bench said the petitioners failed to show that their assignment as BLOs prejudiced their teaching duties or the education of children.
Briefly put, the petition was filed by 5 Assistant Teachers working at Junior/Senior Basic Schools in Saharanpur.
They sought a direction to the authorities to detach them from their duties as BLOs and restrain them from interfering with their discharge of duties as teachers.
It was their contention that there was no provision in the terms and conditions of their service under which they could be assigned BLO duties.

They further argued that such deployment was contrary to Article 21-A of the Constitution, read with the provisions of the RTE Act and the Rules framed thereunder, as it diverted teachers from their core duty of imparting education.
Finding no merits in the petition, the Court noted that the preparation and revision of electoral rolls is a statutory function under the Representation of the People Act, 1950.
It further observed that Article 324 of the Constitution vests the superintendence, direction and control of elections in the Election Commission of India.

The Court also referred to Section 13CC of the 1950 Act, under which officers and staff of the State Government and local authorities employed in the preparation, revision and correction of electoral rolls are deemed to be on deputation to the Election Commission for that period.

stories.headline: Trump 2.0 and the Changing Trade Winds: Is India Ready to Lead?
stories.title: Trump 2.0 and the Changing Trade Winds: Is India Ready to Lead?
stories.summary: As the world gets ready for Donald Trump's return to the White House on January 20th with a potential of China facing tariffs that may negatively impact its trade dominance globally, a new question comes forth: Can India rise to seize the emerging opportunities in the west ? The trade landscape is changing in global perspectives. China's trade surplus recently passed $1 trillion, drawing many countries into its economic influence. However, this has raised concerns in Western economies, especially in Europe, which is now rethinking its dependence on Chinese imports. Donald Trump, who during his first term launched a trade war with China, appears to refuel itself under similar guidelines. His narrative of inducing tariffs on Chinese goods not only makes his supporters happy but also aligns with the Western commercial market hoping to diversify their supply chains. This changing dynamic creates new game plan for countries like India. Europe’s anxiety over its dependence on China has grown over the past few years, especially since the COVID-19 pandemic exposed susceptibilities in the international supply chains. As talks regarding “de-risking” from China escalate, European nations are actively looking for alternative trade partners. India, with its rising economy, production, vibrant tech sector, and massive workforce for sure is an absolute candidate to fill the vacuum. A simple example of this would be, Anker, world’s leading mobile charging company that has recently decided of sourcing lithium cells from India. However, the question that comes forward: Is India prepared to capitalize on this moment? Despite India's economy has shown pliability, infrastructure continues to be an important barrier. India will need to ensure significant investments in rebuilding its infrastructure if it is to successfully compete with China's highly efficient transport and supply chain systems. The "Make in India" campaign has boosted India and changed the mentality of Indians into relying on and acceptance of foreign products. This drive which is also stemmed from a nationalistic Indian vision has done one thing for sure, promoted indigenous and regional manufacturing. However, compared to China, its output is still low. India should boost its manufacturing capabilities in order to become a competitive and more convincing alternative, guaranteeing both quantity and quality that satisfies the western and the European norms. Moreover, to keep the manufacturing strength of India run smooth, the GOI at the same time should also place its focus into the simplification of taxation and labour laws. India has a significant advantage due to its growing and more importantly young population, also referred to as the demographic dividend. However, the nation must concentrate on equipping its people to become more efficient and meet the demands of manufacturing. Moreover, India still faces major obstacles in its acquisition of skilled workers as of 2022. According to the Ministry of Skill Development and Entrepreneurship study less than 5% of India's workforce obtains formal skills training, comparison to nations like Germany which is over 70%. India needs to step up its efforts at vocational training and up skilling, if it wants to stay competitive in the global market, especially in high-tech industries. While India visions itself as a recipient of being a developed nation by 2047, she has a bright future and a long road ahead, filled with obstacles and opportunities. One such arena of potential growth is the western emphasis on eco-friendly renewable energy better known as the European Green Deal, aiming for climate neutrality by 2050. India on the other hand, is well-positioned to take advantage of this demand keeping in mind, its growing vision in solar energy, wind power, and electric mobility. It would be unfair to mention its ambition. According to the Ministry of New and Renewable Energy, India projects on “achieving 500 GW of installed electric capacity from non-fossil sources by 2030”. It is noteworthy to mention the uneasy setting between the ever-competing global ideologies of democracy and communism, rooted in the Cold War era with Soviet times in Afghanistan and the further intervention of the US. In this context, India serves as an alternative to China's growing influence in the Asian region. As the largest democracy of the continent, India's political values align more closely with the west, making it a suitable diplomatically in efforts to maintain regional stability. In conclusion, Donald Trump’s re-entry into the Oval Office may signal renewed trade tensions between the US and China. Nevertheless, this comes with paired opportunities for India: to site itself as a reliable and an efficient alternative to China and to make stronger trade ties with both the US and the Europe. However, this snatch requires more than just ambition; it requires a coordinated and collective effort to overcome infrastructure, improve manufacturing and accelerate trade negotiations. India’s keenness to flourish on this juncture monetarily while changing the global perception towards the Indian market will undergo a metamorphosis, from being looked as underdog, to now being perceived as the big giant. This will further shape the new India’s role in the global economy for years to come. With the right investments and policies, India could emerge not just as a substitute to China, but also as a global trade leader. (The Author is PhD International Relations. Feedback: Aman.jaswal@staffs.ac.uk )

article_sentences: - Death toll in Old Delhi building collapse rises to three after another labourer's body is recovered.
- Five people rescued so far, including two injured workers who are stable.
- Police book building owners and contractors for culpable homicide; unauthorised construction had been flagged in June.

The death toll in the three-storey building collapse in Old Delhi's Hauz Qazi area rose to three on Saturday, 7 November after rescuers recovered the body of another worker from the debris, nearly 48 hours after the incident.
The deceased has been identified as Pankaj Sharma (40), a resident of Hanuman Nagar village in Bihar's Khagaria district, officials said.
Five people have so far been pulled out of the rubble — three dead and two injured.
Both survivors have received medical treatment and are reported to be stable.
Rescue operations and efforts to clear the debris were continuing at the site.
The under-construction building collapsed in Gali Sitara, near Chawri Bazar Metro station, around 9.45 am on Thursday, 5 November.
Between 10 and 15 labourers were present at the construction site when the three-storey structure came crashing down, deputy commissioner of police (central) Rohit Rajbir Singh had said.
Earlier, two labourers identified as Kishori (40) and Sanjeet (45) were declared dead.
Two others, Sahdev Chaudhary (25) and Firoz (37), were rescued with injuries.

article_sentences: The Supreme Court on November 2, 2026 described bursting of firecrackers during Deepavali as a “religious practice” while permitting the use of green firecrackers for two days, on November 7 and November 8, in Delhi-NCR.

The unregulated use of firecrackers during Deepavali has historically led to a sharp rise in the Air Quality Index (AQI) and pollution levels, including the emission of particulate matter, the court observed.

“The right of an individual to engage in a particular practice, which may have a religious colour, is only a qualified one and cannot go beyond the Constitutional restrictions,” the Supreme Court held.
The state had “utterly failed” to comply with the Supreme Court’s orders issued since 2015 to impose restrictions on fireworks, the Bench said.
In fact, the situation had not improved even after the reimposition of a complete ban on firecrackers.
A significant spike in AQI levels was noticed on Dasara and the following day.
The “complete ban” had not only facilitated the illegal sale of firecrackers but had also prevented people from purchasing authorised green crackers, the court said.
The court had earlier suggested that the government enlist celebrities such as cricketer Virat Kohli to spread awareness about the harmful effects of firecrackers.

In October 2025, the apex court had permitted the sale and bursting of green firecrackers in Delhi-NCR during Deepavali, subject to conditions aimed at balancing tradition with environmental and health concerns.
The court had then made it clear that the use of green crackers would be restricted to specified hours on the festival day and its eve.

The court permitted the bursting of certified green firecrackers between 6 a.m. and 7 a.m. and between 8 p.m. and 10 p.m. on November 7, 2026 and the day after in the Delhi National Capital Region (Delhi-NCR).

The “complete ban” had not only facilitated the illegal sale of firecrackers but had also prevented people from purchasing authorised green crackers, the court said.
The court had earlier suggested that the government enlist celebrities such as cricketer Virat Kohli to spread awareness about the harmful effects of firecrackers.

In October 2025, the apex court had permitted the sale and bursting of green firecrackers in Delhi-NCR during Deepavali, subject to conditions aimed at balancing tradition with environmental and health concerns.
The court had then made it clear that the use of green crackers would be restricted to specified hours on the festival day and its eve.

stories.headline: Former Supreme Court judge Justice Rajesh Bindal appointed NCLAT chairperson, ending interim arrangement
stories.title: Former Supreme Court judge Justice Rajesh Bindal appointed NCLAT chairperson, ending interim arrangement
stories.summary: New Delhi, Nov 07: Former Supreme Court judge Justice Rajesh Bindal has been appointed chairperson of the National Company Law Appellate Tribunal (NCLAT), filling the key position that had been held on an officiating basis since July 2026, according to a report by Livelaw. Justice Bindal, who served as a judge of the Supreme Court from February 13, 2023, to April 15, 2026, succeeds the interim arrangement under which Justice Yogesh Khanna had been discharging the duties of NCLAT chairperson following the completion of Justice Ashok Bhushan's tenure. Justice Bindal brings with him extensive judicial experience across several High Courts. He was elevated to the Punjab and Haryana High Court in 2006 before being transferred to the Jammu and Kashmir High Court in 2018. During his tenure in Jammu and Kashmir, he also served as the Acting Chief Justice of the High Court in December 2020. Subsequently, he was transferred to the Calcutta High Court in January 2021 and assumed charge as its Acting Chief Justice in April 2021. He took the oath as Chief Justice of the Allahabad High Court on October 11, 2021, before his elevation to the Supreme Court in 2023. After retiring from the Supreme Court, he was appointed as Emeritus Professor at the National Forensic Sciences University (NFSU) and joined Galgotias University School of Law as an Honorary Distinguished Jurist. His appointment marks the end of the interim arrangement at the appellate tribunal, which deals with appeals arising from orders passed by the National Company Law Tribunal (NCLT).

stories.headline: Planning to invest in gold and silver this Diwali? 7 experts decode the risks, outlook and allocation strategy
stories.title: Planning to invest in gold and silver this Diwali? 7 experts decode the risks, outlook and allocation strategy
stories.summary: Buying gold and silver during Diwali is a long-standing tradition in India, with many investors also viewing the festive season as an opportunity to review their portfolios and consider fresh investments in precious metals. However, after a strong rally followed by a sharp correction in 2026, investors may be wondering whether to add to their gold and silver holdings, wait for prices to stabilise or rebalance their existing exposure.Experts believe that while gold and silver continue to have a role in portfolios, investors should be mindful of near-term volatility, interest rate movements and their overall asset allocation. Their views differ on the preferred metal and the ideal allocation, but they broadly emphasise the importance of avoiding momentum-driven decisions.What is driving gold and silver prices?Gold and silver prices have faced pressure from rising energy prices, inflation concerns and hawkish signals from the US Federal Reserve. These developments have reduced expectations of monetary easing and weighed on precious metals.Also Read | Gold vs silver ETFs: Which metal offers better opportunity for investors this Diwali?Rahul Khetawat, Senior Vice President and Fund Manager at 360 ONE Asset, said that the key factors to watch in FY27 include signals from the US Federal Reserve on interest rates and inflation, as well as developments towards a resolution of the conflict in the Middle East. Central bank purchases and investment demand continue to provide support to precious metals.Tapan Patel, Fund Manager – Commodities at Tata Asset Management, said that inflation, elevated yields and central bank tightening have dominated the short-term outlook, despite supportive long-term factors. However, he believes concerns around global growth, central bank diversification, de-dollarisation and US fiscal sustainability could continue to support long-term investment demand for gold and silver.Patel also pointed to the impact of geopolitical uncertainty and changing weather patterns on commodity prices. He said investors have increasingly recognised the benefits of having commodity exposure in their portfolios.While both metals have a place in portfolios, some experts currently favour gold over silver. Khetawat said 360 ONE Asset's portfolio positioning is tilted towards gold. Given the prevailing macroeconomic and geopolitical uncertainties, the fund house prefers a measured allocation to precious metals, with a relatively larger share in gold.He believes gold may offer better risk-reward in the current environment because of inflation concerns, geopolitical risks and broader macroeconomic uncertainty. Silver may also present opportunities, but its price movements are influenced by industrial demand and broader economic activity, apart from investment flows.Satish Dondapati, Fund Manager at Kotak Mahindra AMC, said gold prices have corrected nearly 3% in US dollar terms over the past week, touching their lowest level in almost a year. Softer US bond yields and a weaker dollar could support prices, but the Federal Reserve's hawkish stance and expectations of higher interest rates for longer have kept gold under pressure.He added that the ongoing Iran conflict has disrupted global energy markets, keeping crude oil prices elevated and adding to inflation concerns. Despite these geopolitical risks, gold has struggled to gain support as markets remain focused on the US Federal Reserve's interest rate outlook.Dondapati believes gold may remain under pressure in the near term, with further volatility possible. He advised investors against deploying the entire investment amount at current levels and suggested staggered buying during price declines. However, he said gold can continue to form part of a long-term portfolio as a hedge against uncertainty and for diversification.Should investors buy more gold after the correction?Kalpen Parekh of DSP Mutual Fund cautioned investors against increasing exposure to gold simply because it has delivered strong returns in recent years.He said gold should be viewed as a portfolio diversifier rather than an asset in which investors should keep chasing returns. Unlike equities, gold does not have underlying earnings or cash flows, and its price is influenced by global uncertainty, interest rates, currencies and investor demand.Also Read | SIFs gain investor traction with over Rs 38,000 crore in assets. Should investors add them to their portfolios this Diwali?Parekh said investors who are underweight on gold may find the recent 25% correction a relatively better opportunity to add to their allocation. However, those whose gold exposure has increased significantly following the rally may consider rebalancing some of their holdings into other asset classes.He added that investors do not need to exit gold or keep adding to it based on recent price movements. The objective of asset allocation is to hold different asset classes that behave differently across market cycles, rather than continuously moving money into investments that have recently performed well.How much should investors allocate to gold and silver?Abhisek Bahinipati, Head – Passive Investments at Invesco Mutual Fund, said that an allocation of around 15% of a portfolio to precious metals may be sensible for most investors. Within this allocation, he suggested keeping roughly two-thirds in gold and one-third in silver. This would translate into an allocation of about 10% to gold and 5% to silver.More conservative investors may consider limiting silver exposure to around 3%, given its higher volatility. Younger investors with longer investment horizons may be able to take a slightly higher allocation to silver, he said.Bahinipati cited a portfolio comprising 60% equity, 25% debt and 15% silver, which delivered a return of 12.4% between Diwali 2025 and September 2026, compared with 8.2% for a traditional 65:35 equity-debt portfolio. The portfolio with silver exposure also generated a higher Sharpe ratio, indicating better risk-adjusted returns.He said investors should first define their target allocation and use it to guide their decisions. If gold and silver have grown beyond their intended portfolio weight because of price appreciation, investors may consider trimming the excess and reallocating it to asset classes where they are underweight. If the allocation remains within the desired range, staying invested may be a better option.What is the outlook for gold and silver?The near-term outlook remains uncertain as precious metals face competing forces. Higher interest rates and bond yields make non-yielding assets such as gold and silver less attractive, while central bank purchases, investment demand and geopolitical uncertainty provide longer-term support.Motilal Oswal Private Wealth said higher yields, a firm dollar and the possibility of tighter monetary policy could continue to create short-term volatility in gold prices. Recent US inflation data have also kept the possibility of further Federal Reserve tightening alive.However, the firm noted that demand for gold is broadening. Central banks continue to accumulate reserves, ETF holdings have reached record levels, and concerns around fiscal sustainability and sovereign debt are encouraging investors to hold assets without an issuer or counterparty risk. It therefore maintains a Neutral allocation to gold.Also Read | Quant Small Cap Fund adds Jio Platforms and 4 others; increases stake in Adani Power, 5 moreNuvama Wealth Research cautioned that a sharp correction in precious metals could trigger liquidation and eventually redirect liquidity towards equities as relative valuations become attractive.Bahinipati said the longer-term outlook for both metals remains constructive, even though volatility may persist in the near term. He pointed out that central banks purchased 244 tonnes of gold in the first quarter of 2026 alone. Silver, meanwhile, is on track for its sixth consecutive year of supply deficit, with industrial applications accounting for around 58% of total demand, driven by sectors such as solar power, electric vehicles and electronics.For Indian investors, a weaker rupee could provide an additional layer of support to precious metals returns, he said.How should investors approach gold and silver this Diwali?Patel suggested that investors look beyond gold and silver and consider building a diversified commodity allocation as part of their portfolios. He said investors can access commodities through registered commodity exchanges, ETFs, Sovereign Gold Bonds and mutual fund schemes offering commodity exposure.Some asset management companies also offer commodity exposure through hybrid and multi-asset schemes, while certain exchange-traded commodity derivatives strategies provide exposure to a wider range of commodities.Bahinipati said investors should focus on gradual accumulation and disciplined asset allocation rather than trying to predict short-term price movements.(Disclaimer: Recommendations, suggestions, views and opinions given by the experts are their own. opening: Buying gold and silver during Diwali is a long-standing tradition in India, with many investors also viewing the festive season as an opportunity to review their portfolios and consider fresh investments in precious metals.

However, after a strong rally followed by a sharp correction in 2026, investors may be wondering whether to add to their gold and silver holdings, wait for prices to stabilise or rebalance their existing exposure.
body: Experts believe that while gold and silver continue to have a role in portfolios, investors should be mindful of near-term volatility, interest rate movements and their overall asset allocation.
Their views differ on the preferred metal and the ideal allocation, but they broadly emphasise the importance of avoiding momentum-driven decisions.
What is driving gold and silver prices?
Gold and silver prices have faced pressure from rising energy prices, inflation concerns and hawkish signals from the US Federal Reserve.
These developments have reduced expectations of monetary easing and weighed on precious metals..
Central bank purchases and investment demand continue to provide support to precious metals.

Tapan Patel, Fund Manager – Commodities at Tata Asset Management, said that inflation, elevated yields and central bank tightening have dominated the short-term outlook, despite supportive long-term factors.

However, he believes concerns around global growth, central bank diversification, de-dollarisation and US fiscal sustainability could continue to support long-term investment demand for gold and silver.
Patel also pointed to the impact of geopolitical uncertainty and changing weather patterns on commodity prices.
He said investors have increasingly recognised the benefits of having commodity exposure in their portfolios.
While both metals have a place in portfolios, some experts currently favour gold over silver.
Khetawat said 360.
ONE Asset's portfolio positioning is tilted towards gold.
Given the prevailing macroeconomic and geopolitical uncertainties, the fund house prefers a measured allocation to precious metals, with a relatively larger share in gold.
He believes gold may offer better risk-reward in the current environment because of inflation concerns, geopolitical risks and broader macroeconomic uncertainty.
Silver may also present opportunities, but its price movements are influenced by industrial demand and broader economic activity, apart from investment flows.
Satish Dondapati, Fund Manager at Kotak Mahindra AMC, said gold prices have corrected nearly 3% in US dollar terms over the past week, touching their lowest level in almost a year.
Softer US bond yields and a weaker dollar could support prices, but the Federal Reserve's hawkish stance and expectations of higher interest rates for longer have kept gold under pressure.
He added that the ongoing Iran conflict has disrupted global energy markets, keeping crude oil prices elevated and adding to inflation concerns.
Despite these geopolitical risks, gold has struggled to gain support as markets remain focused on the US Federal Reserve's interest rate outlook.
Dondapati believes gold may remain under pressure in the near term, with further volatility possible.
He advised investors against deploying the entire investment amount at current levels and suggested staggered buying during price declines.
However, he said gold can continue to form part of a long-term portfolio as a hedge against uncertainty and for diversification.
Should investors buy more gold after the correction?
Kalpen Parekh of DSP Mutual Fund cautioned investors against increasing exposure to gold simply because it has delivered strong returns in recent years.
He said gold should be viewed as a portfolio diversifier rather than an asset in which investors should keep chasing returns.
Unlike equities, gold does not have underlying earnings or cash flows, and its price is influenced by global uncertainty, interest rates, currencies and investor demand..
Should investors add them to their portfolios this Diwali?
Parekh said investors who are underweight on gold may find the recent 25% correction a relatively better opportunity to add to their allocation.
However, those whose gold exposure has increased significantly following the rally may consider rebalancing some of their holdings into other asset classes.
He added that investors do not need to exit gold or keep adding to it based on recent price movements.

The objective of asset allocation is to hold different asset classes that behave differently across market cycles, rather than continuously moving money into investments that have recently performed well.
How much should investors allocate to gold and silver?
Within this allocation, he suggested keeping roughly two-thirds in gold and one-third in silver.
More conservative investors may consider limiting silver exposure to around 3%, given its higher volatility.
Younger investors with longer investment horizons may be able to take a slightly higher allocation to silver, he said.

Bahinipati cited a portfolio comprising 60% equity, 25% debt and 15% silver, which delivered a return of 12.4% between Diwali 2025 and September 2026, compared with 8.2% for a traditional 65:35 equity-debt portfolio.
The portfolio with silver exposure also generated a higher Sharpe ratio, indicating better risk-adjusted returns.
He said investors should first define their target allocation and use it to guide their decisions.

If gold and silver have grown beyond their intended portfolio weight because of price appreciation, investors may consider trimming the excess and reallocating it to asset classes where they are underweight.
If the allocation remains within the desired range, staying invested may be a better option.
The near-term outlook remains uncertain as precious metals face competing forces.

Higher interest rates and bond yields make non-yielding assets such as gold and silver less attractive, while central bank purchases, investment demand and geopolitical uncertainty provide longer-term support.
Motilal Oswal Private Wealth said higher yields, a firm dollar and the possibility of tighter monetary policy could continue to create short-term volatility in gold prices.
Recent US inflation data have also kept the possibility of further Federal Reserve tightening alive.
However, the firm noted that demand for gold is broadening.

Central banks continue to accumulate reserves, ETF holdings have reached record levels, and concerns around fiscal sustainability and sovereign debt are encouraging investors to hold assets without an issuer or counterparty risk.
It therefore maintains a Neutral allocation to gold.
Nuvama Wealth Research cautioned that a sharp correction in precious metals could trigger liquidation and eventually redirect liquidity towards equities as relative valuations become attractive.
Bahinipati said the longer-term outlook for both metals remains constructive, even though volatility may persist in the near term.
He pointed out that central banks purchased 244 tonnes of gold in the first quarter of 2026 alone.

Silver, meanwhile, is on track for its sixth consecutive year of supply deficit, with industrial applications accounting for around 58% of total demand, driven by sectors such as solar power, electric vehicles and electronics.
For Indian investors, a weaker rupee could provide an additional layer of support to precious metals returns, he said.
How should investors approach gold and silver this Diwali?
Patel suggested that investors look beyond gold and silver and consider building a diversified commodity allocation as part of their portfolios.
He said investors can access commodities through registered commodity exchanges, ETFs, Sovereign Gold Bonds and mutual fund schemes offering commodity exposure.

Some asset management companies also offer commodity exposure through hybrid and multi-asset schemes, while certain exchange-traded commodity derivatives strategies provide exposure to a wider range of commodities.

stories.title: Noel Tata to step down as Voltas chairman, appointed Chairman Emeritus
stories.summary: Noel N Tata, Chairman of Tata Trusts, has been appointed as Chairman Emeritus of Voltas, a day after he retired as Chairman and Director of the leading cooling products maker. Noel Tata will retire as Chairman and Director of Voltas Ltd on November 11, 2026, upon attaining the age of superannuation under Tata Group governance guidelines. Following his retirement, "the Board has appointed him as Chairman Emeritus of the Company with effect from November 12, 2026," said Voltas, a Tata Group firm, in its regulatory filing. The Companies Act 2013 mandates that any managing director or whole-time director cannot be appointed or continue employment if they are 70 years of age or older. Noel Tata, who was born on November 12, 1956, will turn 70 on November 12, 2026. He has been associated with Voltas since 2003. Additionally, the board has appointed Sunil D'Souza as the new Chairman of Voltas. D'Souza currently leads the Tata Group's FMCG arm, Tata Consumer Products Ltd (TCPL), as Mana

stories.summary: The Bench highlighted the large number of vehicles plying on roads connecting Delhi with neighbouring areas, including Ghaziabad, Greater Noida, Gurugram and Faridabad

article_sentences: The Supreme Court on Friday (November 6, 2026) termed vehicular emissions a major contributor to air pollution in Delhi-NCR and said immediate, medium- and long-term measures were needed to curb the rising air quality index.

Hearing a suo motu case examining the regulatory framework governing air pollution, a Bench comprising Chief Justice of India Surya Kant and Justices Joymalya Bagchi and V. Mohana also expressed concern over “bumper-to-bumper” traffic in Delhi-NCR.
“We keep talking and sometimes make statements and suggestions, but the point is that AQI is already touching 400,” the CJI said.
The Bench highlighted the large number of vehicles plying on roads connecting Delhi with neighbouring areas, including Ghaziabad, Greater Noida, Gurugram and Faridabad.
“Look at the roads in Delhi and the roads connecting Delhi with the NCR.
Take a look at any road and the kind of vehicles moving on it.
That is the major problem,” the CJI said.
The Bench said the poor people are the real sufferers, as they are on the roads, and moreover, the festival time is the only period when they earn a livelihood.
On stubble burning, the Bench stressed the need to educate farmers about using machines instead of resorting to farm fires.

On the plea seeking closure of schools or running them in hybrid mode for students of all age groups if the air quality index (AQI) rises above a certain mark, the bench said it will go by experts’ opinion.

Additional Solicitor General Aishwarya Bhati, appearing for the Centre and other authorities, referred to the regulatory framework covering five major sectors: industrial emissions, vehicular pollution, construction and demolition dust, road dust and stubble burning.

She told the Bench that several measures had been introduced, including restrictions on the entry of certain vehicles, geo-tagging of pollution under control (PUC) certificates and action against visibly polluting vehicles through complaints received on applications and social media.
